discrete_risks.name: A new record warmest calendar year, exceeding 2024
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: Copernicus ERA5 (with NASA GISTEMP and NOAA as corroboration) reports a calendar year with a global mean surface temperature anomaly exceeding the 2024 value (1.60C above 1850-1900) at the annual announcement in the following January.
discrete_risks.reasoning: A very strong El Nino peaking Oct-Dec 2026 delivers its maximum global temperature effect with a ~6-12 month lag, making 2027 the leading candidate, exactly as 2016 followed the 2015-16 event. Underlying forced warming has added roughly 0.05C since 2024. Carbon Brief already gives 2026 alone a 35% record chance and Polymarket prices ~31%; 2027 is materially higher. WMO's Global Annual to Decadal Update independently gives 86% that some year in 2026-2030 beats 2024.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: years since 1980 that set a new annual global record. 12 of 46 years (1981, 1983, 1987, 1988, 1990, 1995, 1997, 1998, 2005, 2010, 2014, 2015, 2016, 2023, 2024) - roughly 30% unconditionally, but conditional on the year following a very strong El Nino peak the hit rate is 3 of 3 (1983, 1998, 2016).
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: El Nino forecasts made in July for a December peak have busted badly before - 2014 is the canonical case, where a forecast super event fizzled and the record slipped a year. If the event peaks at only moderate-to-strong (+1.2 to +1.5C ONI) and the post-2023 albedo anomaly partially relaxes, 2027 could land near 1.55C and fall short of 2024. There is also a real chance the 2023-24 spike was partly a transient (Hunga Tonga water vapour, IMO 2020 sulphur, unusually low cloud cover) that does not repeat.

discrete_risks.name: A calendar year at or above 1.65C above pre-industrial
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: ERA5 annual global mean surface temperature anomaly relative to 1850-1900 is >= 1.65C for a full calendar year, as published in the Copernicus Global Climate Highlights.
discrete_risks.reasoning: 2024 reached 1.60C in ERA5 on the back of a moderate-to-strong El Nino plus anomalous forcing. Forced warming has added ~0.05-0.07C since. A very strong El Nino should deliver an additional 0.1-0.2C in the lag year, putting the 2027 central estimate around 1.68C with a standard deviation of roughly 0.09C. By the early 2030s the trend alone (0.025C/yr) reaches this level even in ENSO-neutral years.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: the observed ERA5 sequence 2023 (1.48), 2024 (1.60), 2025 (~1.53-1.55), H1 2026 (~1.40). Crossing 1.65C has never happened; the step from 1.60 to 1.65 is one El Nino amplitude plus two years of trend.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: If the El Nino underdelivers and the 2023-24 anomalous forcing (reduced planetary albedo, low low-cloud cover) reverses, annual anomalies could plateau near 1.5-1.6C for several years. Several groups argue the 2023-24 jump exceeded what CMIP models predicted and is partly unexplained, which cuts both ways: unexplained warming may be transient rather than a new baseline.

discrete_risks.name: Long-term (multi-decadal) 1.5C breach formally declared
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: The WMO, IPCC (in AR7 or a special report), or the UNFCCC Global Stocktake formally states that the long-term global mean temperature increase - defined as a 20-year mean or current human-induced warming - has exceeded 1.5C above 1850-1900.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Indicators of Global Climate Change assessments put current human-induced warming at roughly 1.36C in 2024, rising at ~0.27C/decade. Central crossing of the 1.5C decadal-mean line lands around 2029-2031. Institutional declaration lags the physical crossing by 2-4 years because 20-year centred means require future data and because the political cost of declaring is high. AR7 (expected ~2028) and the second Global Stocktake (2028) are the natural declaration venues.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: institutional acknowledgement of previously-crossed climate thresholds. The 400 ppm CO2 threshold was crossed in 2013-2016 and acknowledged within about a year; the 1.0C threshold was crossed around 2015 and acknowledged by WMO the same year. But 1.5C carries treaty consequences, which historically slows formal acknowledgement.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Institutions may deliberately avoid a binary declaration to preserve the Paris framing of 'limiting to 1.5C with overshoot and return', in which case the event never resolves yes even as the physical threshold is unambiguously crossed. Alternatively, definitional choices - which baseline, which dataset, whether to include natural variability - could keep the headline number below 1.5C into the mid-2030s.

discrete_risks.name: The 2026-27 El Nino verifies as very strong (ONI peak >= +2.0C)
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: NOAA CPC's Oceanic Nino Index (3-month running mean Nino3.4 anomaly, ERSSTv5 with the operational base period) reaches or exceeds +2.0C for at least one overlapping season during the 2026-27 event.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Verified: NOAA declared a Super El Nino on 11 June 2026 with a 63% chance of 'very strong'; CPC gives 96% El Nino for DJF 2026-27; all 30 GFDL SPEAR members peak competitive with the strongest events of the past century; 23 of 26 models forecast very strong for OND 2026. Forecasts issued in July for a Nov-Dec peak have crossed the spring predictability barrier and are far more skillful than April forecasts. I am discounting the headline ECMWF median of +3.0C and the circulating multi-model figure of +3.59C because no observed event has exceeded ~+2.75C and dynamical models systematically overshoot in the upper tail.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: ONI peaks >= +2.0C since 1950 - 1972-73, 1982-83, 1997-98, 2015-16, and arguably 1991-92. That is 4-5 events in 76 years, roughly 6% per year unconditionally. Conditional on a July forecast with near-unanimous multi-model very-strong support, the historical hit rate is roughly 3 of 4.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: The 2014 forecast bust is the direct counterexample: a strongly-supported super El Nino forecast collapsed into a weak event when the westerly wind bursts failed to materialize. Atmospheric coupling can decouple from a warm subsurface. Also, the ONI's shifting 30-year base period mechanically suppresses anomalies relative to older events, so a physically comparable event could score below +2.0C on the operational index - a resolution trap worth noting.

discrete_risks.name: Bleaching-level heat stress affects >= 60% of global reef area within a 12-month window
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: NOAA Coral Reef Watch reports that Alert Level 1 or higher bleaching-level heat stress affected at least 60% of the world's coral reef area within any rolling 12-month period.
discrete_risks.reasoning: The fourth global bleaching event remains active and has already affected 84.4% of reef area cumulatively since January 2023. A very strong El Nino peaking December 2026 loads the 2027 Southern Hemisphere season with maximum thermal stress across the Great Barrier Reef, Coral Triangle and western Indian Ocean simultaneously. Every strong El Nino since 1998 has coincided with a global bleaching event. Baseline ocean heat content is at a record for the ninth straight year, so the thermal starting point is higher than in 2015-16.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: global bleaching events - 1998, 2010, 2014-17, 2023-present. Four in 28 years, but 3 of 4 were El Nino-triggered, and the 12-month footprint has grown each time. From 2018 through 2025, 87% of reef area experienced bleaching-level stress with median heat accumulation ~50% above any previous event.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: El Nino cools some reef regions (notably the western Pacific and parts of the Coral Triangle) even as it heats the eastern Pacific and Caribbean, so peak stress can be regionally offset rather than globally synchronized. NOAA's reporting methodology has also changed during the fourth event, and a 60% single-year threshold has only clearly been exceeded once or twice in the satellite record.

discrete_risks.name: Global fossil CO2 emissions confirmed to have peaked
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: The Global Carbon Project reports global fossil CO2 emissions below the previous all-time high in two consecutive calendar years, with the peak year identified in the published Global Carbon Budget.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Verified: 2025 fossil CO2 hit a record 38.1 GtCO2 (+1.1%), but IEA reports energy CO2 growth slowed to +0.4% and forecasts power-sector emissions plateauing 2026-2030. China - roughly 32% of global emissions - fell 0.3% in 2025 and has been flat-or-falling for 21 months, with peaks already reached in power, steel, cement and oil products (>80% of its fossil CO2). India was flat for the first time since the 1970s. The offsetting growth is aviation (+6.8%), petrochemicals and data-centre load. A confirmed two-year decline before 2028 is unlikely; late-decade is the modal peak.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: global fossil CO2 declines lasting two or more consecutive years since 1950 - only 1980-83 (oil shock recession) and effectively never otherwise; 2009 and 2020 were single-year shocks followed by rebound. So structural, non-recessionary two-year declines have a base rate of zero, which argues for humility on the near-term horizon while clean-energy S-curves argue for the 2030s.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Two failure modes. First, electricity demand growth from AI data centres, industrial electrification and air conditioning in a super-El-Nino-warmed world could outrun clean supply additions for years, extending the plateau into the 2030s. Second, the reverse: if China's decline accelerates and India's flatness holds, a peak could already have occurred in 2025 and simply not be confirmable until the 2028 Global Carbon Budget - meaning the 2031 probability could be too low, not too high.

discrete_risks.name: Observed AMOC weakening of >= 30% below the 2004-2023 mean, sustained 12 months
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: The RAPID-MOCHA-WBTS array at 26N (or a successor observing system accepted as the reference by the AMOC research community) reports a 12-month running mean overturning transport at least 30% below the 2004-2023 mean, confirmed in a peer-reviewed publication.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Verified: a 2026 EGUsphere opinion piece argues the AMOC-is-weakening evidence should now be taken seriously and a 2026 review found the bistability evidence base has broadened; a 2026 Communications Earth & Environment paper found collapse would be irreversible above 350 ppm CO2. But a 2026 Science Advances study incorporating Greenland meltwater found no tipping point in sight. RAPID shows large interannual variability (individual years have dipped substantially) but no 30% sustained departure. Proxy-based estimates suggest ~15% weakening since the mid-20th century, i.e. roughly 0.15%/yr - too slow to reach 30% below the modern mean by 2036 absent a nonlinear event.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: 22 years of continuous RAPID observation (2004-2026). The largest sustained anomaly on record is roughly a 10-15% multi-year dip around 2009-2010, which subsequently recovered. Zero instances of a sustained 30% departure in the instrumental era.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: The strongest argument that this is too low: several 2024-2026 papers find early-warning signals of critical slowing down and argue the mid-century tipping window is live, and a 30% weakening is a waypoint on that path rather than the endpoint. The strongest argument it is too high: RAPID has funding fragility, the array could lapse and leave the question unresolvable, and much of the claimed weakening rests on SST-fingerprint proxies that several groups dispute as confounded by aerosol forcing.

discrete_risks.name: AMOC declared to have crossed a tipping point
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: A major assessment body (IPCC, WMO, or a National Academies-equivalent) or a strong majority of the published AMOC literature states that the AMOC has crossed a critical threshold and is on an irreversible trajectory toward collapse (maximum strength below 5 Sv) under current forcing.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Even the pessimistic 2024-2026 modelling literature places the central tipping window in the 2040s-2070s, and detection requires either an unambiguous observational collapse signature or a decisive shift in model consensus. Institutional bodies are structurally conservative about declaring irreversibility. The 2026 Greenland meltwater study explicitly found no near-term tipping point.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: formal scientific declarations that a major Earth-system tipping element has irreversibly tipped. Count in the modern era: arguably zero (West Antarctic marine ice sheet instability has been described as 'possibly past the point of no return' in specific basins, but never formally declared basin-wide). Base rate of such declarations is on the order of once per several decades per element.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: The honest contrarian case is that the literature is moving faster than institutional consensus and that a cluster of high-profile 2027-2030 papers plus a genuine RAPID excursion could produce a rapid cascade of scientific opinion - the 'evidence base has broadened' framing in 2026 reviews is exactly what precedes such a shift. If AR7 includes even a qualified statement, this could resolve yes on a technicality.

discrete_risks.name: Arctic Ocean practically ice-free (extent below 1.0 million km2)
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: NSIDC daily sea ice extent for the Arctic falls below 1.0 million km2 on at least one day.
discrete_risks.reasoning: September minima have been running roughly 4.2-4.7 million km2 over the past decade with no clear acceleration since 2012's 3.39 million km2 record. Reaching 1.0 million km2 requires roughly a 75% further reduction from current minima - a jump far outside observed interannual variability, requiring either a decade of trend plus an extreme dipole-anomaly summer, or a step change in ice thickness. The 2026 winter maximum tied the record low (14.29 million km2), which loads the dice for thin ice, but winter maximum is a weak predictor of the September minimum.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: 47 years of satellite record. Largest single-year drop was 2012 (-18% below the prior record). Extrapolating the 1979-2026 September trend of roughly -0.08 million km2/yr gives a central ice-free date in the 2050s-2060s; the literature's earliest credible estimates cluster around the 2030s conditional on an extreme year.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Several 2024-2025 papers argue the first ice-free day could arrive before 2030 in the tail, driven by preconditioned thin ice plus a single anomalous summer - a mechanism that behaves like a jump process rather than a trend crossing. If ice volume (not extent) is already close to the threshold, the transition could be abrupt and my 2031 number of 4% could be a factor of two too low.

discrete_risks.name: Verified wet-bulb temperature of 35C sustained for three or more hours
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: A quality-controlled surface station observation (or a national meteorological service's official record) documents a wet-bulb temperature of at least 35.0C sustained for at least three consecutive hours, confirmed in a peer-reviewed publication or by a national met service.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Brief exceedances of TW = 35C have already been documented at a handful of stations (Jacobabad in Pakistan, Ras al Khaimah in the UAE, coastal Persian Gulf sites) for one to two hours, roughly doubling in frequency since 1979. A three-hour sustained event requires a strong marine-influenced heat event in the Persian Gulf, Indus Valley or Red Sea coast. A very strong El Nino typically produces a hot South Asian pre-monsoon the following spring - so the 2027 pre-monsoon is an elevated-risk window. Detection is also limited by sparse instrumentation in exactly the regions most at risk.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: documented TW >= 35C exceedances of any duration, 1979-2023. Roughly 1,000 station-hours globally across ~4.5 decades, concentrated post-2000 and heavily in the Persian Gulf and Indus Valley. Sustained 3-hour exceedances: zero confirmed in the literature to date.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: This may already have happened and gone unrecorded - the Indus Valley, Gulf coast of Iran and parts of the Sahel have poor station coverage and inconsistent QC, so the binding constraint may be measurement rather than physics, making the true probability much higher but the resolvable probability lower. Conversely, sustained 35C TW requires a rare combination of high SST, onshore flow and light winds; the physical persistence barrier is real and 3 hours is a demanding bar.

discrete_risks.name: Single heat event with >= 100,000 attributed excess deaths
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: A peer-reviewed study or national statistical office attributes at least 100,000 excess deaths to a single heat wave or heat season within one country or contiguous region over a window of 90 days or less.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Verified: the June 2026 European heat waves produced over 10,000 officially-reported excess deaths in about a week, with one academic estimate of 20,390, and WWA found the event virtually impossible without climate change. Europe-wide summer 2022 reached roughly 62,000. A 100,000-death single event most plausibly requires South Asia or China, where population exposure is an order of magnitude larger but attribution infrastructure is far weaker. A post-super-El-Nino 2027 South Asian pre-monsoon is the highest-risk single window in the near term.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: single heat events with >50,000 attributed excess deaths - Europe 2003 (~70,000), Russia 2010 (~55,000), Europe 2022 (~62,000), Europe 2023 (~47,000). Four in 25 years, roughly 16%/yr for the >50k class; crossing 100,000 has never occurred, requiring roughly a 1.5-2x jump on the worst observed.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Attribution methodology is the binding constraint, not mortality. Europe's excess-death surveillance is uniquely good, which is why European events dominate the record; India and China almost certainly already experience heat mortality of this scale but do not measure or publish it. So the event may be physically likely and epistemically unlikely. Working the other way: adaptation - air conditioning penetration, heat action plans, early warning - has measurably cut heat mortality per degree in Europe and India over the past decade, and that trend is strong.

discrete_risks.name: State-backed solar radiation management deployment announced or conducted
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: A national government formally announces a stratospheric aerosol injection deployment programme (as distinct from research), or a state or state-backed entity conducts SAI at a scale exceeding 0.1 Tg of injected aerosol precursor per year, as confirmed by independent monitoring or official statement.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Verified: the CBD de facto moratorium remains in force and was reinforced by the ICJ's 2025 advisory opinion, which the CIEL analysis reads as counselling precaution against new technologies with serious irreversible harm potential. Stardust Solutions raised $75m and aims to be deployment-ready within a decade but backtracked on planned spring 2026 outdoor experiments. SRM research funding roughly tripled in 2025. The technology is immature at scale and the diplomatic cost to a first mover is severe. Pressure rises sharply if 2027 sets a record year and a lethal heat disaster follows.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: unilateral deployment of a globally-consequential geoengineering technology by a single state against international consensus. Count: zero in history. Nearest analogues - unilateral nuclear testing after the CTBT norm (North Korea, 6 events in 20 years), and unilateral germline editing (He Jiankui 2018, one event) - suggest norm-violating first movers do appear but at rates of order 1-3% per year once capability exists.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: The strongest case that this is too low: a mid-sized state facing existential heat or monsoon disruption (Gulf states, Singapore, or a Sahelian coalition) has both motive and, increasingly, cheap means - the marginal cost of a small SAI programme is low relative to a national climate adaptation budget. Capability is proliferating faster than governance. The case it is too high: 'deployment' is a high bar and the far more likely outcome is a grey zone of escalating private experiments and modelling work that never crosses into anything a neutral judge would call deployment.

discrete_risks.name: Formal international SRM governance decision adopted
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: UNEA, the UNFCCC COP, the CBD COP, or a comparable treaty body adopts a formal decision or instrument establishing an international governance framework for solar radiation modification (whether a non-use agreement, a research governance regime, or a moratorium codification), beyond the existing non-binding CBD language.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Verified: SRM funding roughly tripled in 2025 and startup activity is normalizing the topic, which is exactly the pressure that produces governance responses. UNEA has twice attempted and twice failed to adopt an SRM resolution (2019 and 2024), each time blocked by a coalition including the US and Saudi Arabia. The ICJ advisory opinion gives non-use advocates new legal footing and UNGA resolution A/80/L.65 in May 2026 shows the operationalization machinery is moving. But the US, now outside Paris and with a deregulatory EPA, is a determined blocker of anything binding.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: multilateral environmental governance instruments adopted for an emerging technology within a decade of serious commercial interest. Montreal Protocol (~10 years from the 1974 science), Cartagena Protocol on biosafety (~8 years), ocean fertilization (LC/LP resolution ~7 years from the first commercial ventures). Roughly 2-4%/yr once the issue is on a treaty agenda.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Two failure modes for this forecast. Governance may arrive not as a formal treaty decision but as a soft, non-resolvable patchwork of national research rules and voluntary codes - the most likely real-world outcome and one that would score no. Alternatively, a single alarming unilateral experiment could produce a governance instrument within 18 months, in which case my 2027 number is far too low.

discrete_risks.name: Amazon basin becomes a net annual carbon source for three consecutive years
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: Peer-reviewed literature (atmospheric inversion, aircraft profile, or eddy-covariance synthesis accepted by the Global Carbon Project) establishes that the Amazon basin as a whole was a net annual source of carbon to the atmosphere in three consecutive calendar years.
discrete_risks.reasoning: The southeastern Amazon has already been documented as a net source, and the 2023-24 drought pushed large parts of the basin to source status, but basin-wide multi-year source status has not been established. Verified counterweight: Brazilian deforestation is at an 11-year low (5,796 km2 to July 2025), alerts fell to 1,325 km2 for Aug 2025-Jan 2026, and cumulative reduction since 2022 is roughly 50%. However, a very strong El Nino reliably produces severe Amazon drought and fire in the following year, and fire-driven degradation now exceeds deforestation as a carbon flux. The 2027 fire season is the key risk window.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: years in which the Amazon was assessed as a net annual source. Roughly 2015-16 and 2023-24 in the inversion literature - about 4 of the last 20 years, all El-Nino-drought-associated, and never three consecutive. Three consecutive requires either a multi-year drought regime or a genuine regime shift.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: This could be much higher than I have it: the 'three consecutive years' criterion may already be near-satisfied and simply unmeasured, because basin-wide flux estimates have enormous uncertainty and the observing network (aircraft profiles at four sites) is thin. Alternatively much lower: Brazil's deforestation collapse under Lula, if extended by the October 2026 election, plus CO2 fertilization, could keep the basin a net sink through any single El Nino drought. The October 2026 Brazilian election is close to a binary fork on this variable.

discrete_risks.name: Final court judgment ordering >= $1bn in climate damages
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: A court of final instance (highest domestic court, or a binding international tribunal) issues a non-appealable judgment ordering a state or a company to pay at least US$1 billion in damages, compensation, or a compliance fund specifically for climate change harms.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Verified: the ICJ's July 2025 advisory opinion held unanimously that fossil fuel production, consumption, licensing and subsidies may constitute an internationally wrongful act attributable to a state, and UNGA resolution A/80/L.65 (20 May 2026) operationalized it. Domestic courts in Costa Rica, France, the Netherlands, Brazil and Canada have already cited it. But the pipeline from advisory opinion to a final, non-appealable billion-dollar damages award runs through 5-10 years of appeals. Urgenda and Shell/Milieudefensie produced injunctive relief, not damages. The most likely first vehicle is a Global South state suing a major emitter, or a US state attorney-general climate-deception case.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: mass-tort litigation reaching final billion-dollar judgments. Tobacco took roughly 40 years from first suit to the 1998 MSA; opioids took roughly 15 years; asbestos roughly 25. Climate litigation's first substantive suits date to the mid-2000s, putting the modal first mega-judgment in the late 2020s to 2030s. Roughly 3-4%/yr rising.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Settlements, not judgments, are how these actually resolve - the tobacco MSA and the opioid deals were both settlements, which would score no on a strict reading of 'court judgment'. Also, the US legal environment has moved sharply the other way: the endangerment finding repeal and a conservative Supreme Court majority make a US mega-judgment far less likely than the ICJ momentum suggests. On the other side, the ICJ opinion is a genuine regime change in international law and I may be underweighting how fast national courts in the Netherlands, Brazil and Colombia now move.

discrete_risks.name: Combined Lake Powell + Lake Mead storage falls below 20% of capacity
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: US Bureau of Reclamation end-of-month reservoir reports show combined active storage in Lake Powell and Lake Mead below 20% of combined live capacity.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Verified: Colorado River system storage is around 36% of capacity, 2026 is described as the worst hydrologic year on record with the lowest snowpack on record and record-breaking March heat, the 2007 Interim Guidelines and 2019 DCP expire at end-2026, and the seven basin states have twice missed federal deadlines, with Interior set to impose its own plan by 1 October 2026. The 2022 low reached roughly 26-27%. A second consecutive poor snow year plus El-Nino-related uncertainty in the Upper Basin (El Nino tends to wet the Lower Basin but not reliably the Upper Colorado headwaters) could push below 20% by 2027-28. Emergency conservation and mandated cuts are the main balancing force.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: 26 years of the current megadrought (2000-2026). Combined storage has fallen from ~95% to ~36%, with one approach to ~27% in mid-2022 followed by recovery after the 2023 record snowpack. Roughly one near-miss per 25 years historically, but the trend is strongly downward and the reference class is non-stationary.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: The 2023 snowpack showed how fast a single big year reverses the trajectory - one wet winter added several years of buffer. El Nino winters historically favour above-average precipitation in the Lower Basin and the southern Rockies, so 2026-27 may actually be a recovery year, which is the main argument my 2027 number is too high. Conversely, deadpool politics may force such aggressive mandated cuts that the reservoirs are managed to never reach 20%, meaning the physical event is averted by policy.

discrete_risks.name: FAO Food Price Index exceeds 160 in any month
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: The FAO Food Price Index (nominal, 2014-2016 = 100) records a monthly value above 160.0, exceeding the March 2022 all-time high of 160.3.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Verified: the index was 130.3 in June 2026, up 2.2% year-on-year, with May's 131.2 a three-year high; wheat output is forecast down 4.3% to 806.5 Mt partly on El Nino effects in Australia, and rice down 1.8%. Reaching 160 requires roughly a 23% further rise. A very strong El Nino peaking in December 2026 hits the 2027 harvests in South and Southeast Asia, southern Africa and Australia simultaneously - historically the strongest single climate driver of global food prices. But energy prices and export restrictions, not weather, drove the 2022 record, so a climate-only path to 160 is harder than it looks.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: FAO index months above 150 since 1990 - the 2008 spike (peak ~131 in nominal 2014-16 rebased terms), the 2011 spike (~137), and 2021-22 (peak 160.3). Roughly three episodes in 35 years, and only one crossed 160, all of them involving an energy or war shock alongside weather. Base rate for crossing 160 is roughly 1-2% per year unconditionally, elevated in a super El Nino year.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Global grain stocks are comfortable and 2026 production is forecast as the second-highest in history, only 1.9% below last year's record. Food price spikes since 2007 have been dominated by export bans, fertiliser costs and oil prices rather than yield shortfalls - so an El Nino alone is historically insufficient. The 2015-16 super El Nino coincided with falling, not rising, food prices. That is the single strongest argument these numbers are too high.

discrete_risks.name: Global mean methane annual growth rate falls to zero or below
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: NOAA GML reports a global mean CH4 annual increase of 0.0 ppb or less for a calendar year in its published trends series.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Verified: methane reached ~1938 ppb at Mauna Loa in March 2026 and NOAA describes the increase as more rapid over recent years than at any point in the record. Growth peaked around 15 ppb/yr in 2020-21 and has decelerated to roughly 8-10 ppb/yr but remains firmly positive. Getting to zero requires either a large fall in fossil and agricultural emissions (Global Methane Pledge implementation, satellite-driven leak abatement) or a recovery in OH sink capacity. Tropical wetland emissions have been running high and are El-Nino-sensitive - El Nino typically dries tropical wetlands and reduces their emissions, which is a genuine tailwind for 2027-28.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: calendar years with CH4 growth <= 0 since 1983. Approximately 1999-2006 saw several near-zero or slightly negative years (notably 2000, 2001, 2004, 2005). So roughly 4-5 of 43 years, ~10% unconditionally - but the mechanism that produced that plateau (a stabilization of fossil and agricultural sources) is not currently operating.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Methane's recent acceleration is poorly explained and is variously attributed to tropical wetlands, fossil leakage and a declining OH sink; NOAA CSL's own January 2026 work emphasizes atmospheric chemistry as the underappreciated term. If the OH sink recovers - which is a chemistry question, not an emissions question - growth could fall to zero quickly with no policy change, making 30% by 2036 too low. If the wetland feedback is real and temperature-driven, a record-warm 2027 could push growth back above 15 ppb/yr and this number is far too high.

continuous_variables.name: Annual global mean surface temperature anomaly (ERA5, vs 1850-1900)
continuous_variables.notes: Current value is my estimate for full-year 2026 given H1 at ~1.40C plus El Nino warming in H2. Decompose as forced trend (0.025 C/yr, i.e. 0.25 C/decade, consistent with 2015-2025 observed) plus a mean-reverting ENSO term with sd ~0.09C, NOT a random walk - the vol does not compound. 2031 spread reflects trend uncertainty (sd ~0.04C over 5 years) convolved with the ENSO term. Expect 2027 to be the near-term peak (~1.68C central, sd 0.09) followed by a post-El-Nino dip toward 1.55-1.60 in 2028-29.

continuous_variables.name: Annual mean CO2 concentration at Mauna Loa
continuous_variables.notes: 2026 value is the Met Office forecast (429.4 +/- 0.6). Drift set slightly above the 2026 forecast growth of 2.37 ppm because a very strong El Nino suppresses the tropical land sink for 12-24 months; expect 2027 growth of 3.0-3.6 ppm (the 2016 analogue gave 3.0 ppm, the 1998 analogue 2.9 ppm), then reversion to ~2.3. Vol is dominated by land-sink variability, not emissions variability. This is close to a deterministic ramp - the p10-p90 range is only ~5 ppm.

continuous_variables.name: NOAA global mean atmospheric methane
continuous_variables.notes: Current value inferred: NOAA global mean was 1929.6 ppb in 2024, Mauna Loa read ~1938 ppb in March 2026, and global mean runs slightly below northern-hemisphere sites. Drift of 7.5 ppb/yr reflects deceleration from the 2020-21 peak of ~15 ppb/yr. Wide vol because the driver mix (wetlands vs fossil vs OH sink) is genuinely unresolved. El Nino typically suppresses tropical wetland emissions, so 2027-28 growth may undershoot; a La Nina rebound in 2029-30 could overshoot.

continuous_variables.name: Global fossil CO2 emissions (Global Carbon Project)
continuous_variables.notes: 2025 value verified from Global Carbon Budget 2025. Near-zero drift encodes the plateau: China falling, India flat, offset by aviation (+6.8%), petrochemicals and data-centre load. The distribution is left-skewed by 2031 - the downside tail is a genuine peak-and-decline, the upside tail is demand growth outrunning clean supply. p10-p50 gap (2.7) exceeds p50-p90 gap (1.8) to encode that skew. This is the single most policy-sensitive variable in the domain.

continuous_variables.name: Global mean sea level (satellite altimetry, above 1993 baseline)
continuous_variables.notes: Current value inferred from the ~4.5 mm/yr 2023 rate and 5.9 mm/yr in 2024 applied over the altimetry era. Drift of 5.0 mm/yr incorporates the verified acceleration of 0.83 mm/yr/decade, rising to ~5.4 mm/yr by 2031. Interannual vol is ENSO-driven (El Nino years show elevated GMSL as terrestrial water storage shifts to the ocean, La Nina years show dips). This is the most predictable variable here - the 2031 range is only 12 mm wide. Ice-sheet nonlinearity would only materially widen the distribution past 2040.

continuous_variables.name: Arctic sea ice September minimum extent (NSIDC)
continuous_variables.notes: Current value is my estimate for the 2026 minimum (not yet occurred as of 29 July 2026); recent minima have run 4.2-4.7. The 2026 winter maximum tied the record low at 14.29 million km2, which weakly preconditions a low minimum. Drift is the 2007-2026 trend, notably shallower than the 1996-2012 trend - the 2012 record of 3.39 has not been approached in 14 years, which is the key calibration fact. Vol is dominated by summer atmospheric circulation (dipole anomaly), not thermodynamics.

continuous_variables.name: Annual maximum 3-month ONI (Nino3.4)
continuous_variables.notes: Current value is my central forecast for the 2026-27 peak, discounted from the ECMWF median of +3.0C and the circulating multi-model figure of +3.59C because no observed event has exceeded ~+2.75C and models overshoot in the upper tail. This variable is STRONGLY mean-reverting, not a random walk - implement as an AR(1) with a ~1.5-2 year decorrelation time, plus a tendency toward La Nina in the 1-2 years after a very strong El Nino (1983-84, 1998-99, 2016-17 all flipped negative). The 2031 distribution is essentially the unconditional ENSO climatology, mildly skewed positive.

continuous_variables.name: Share of global reef area under Alert Level 1+ heat stress, rolling 12 months
continuous_variables.notes: Current value is my estimate for the rolling 12 months to mid-2026; the cumulative Jan 2023-Sep 2025 figure of 84.4% is verified but is a cumulative, not a 12-month, measure. Extremely ENSO-coupled: expect 75-90% in the 12 months to mid-2027 under peak El Nino, then a fall toward 35-50% in a neutral or La Nina year. Bounded [0,100] - use a logit transform. The drift term captures the rising thermal baseline (ocean heat content at a record for nine straight years), which raises the floor even in cool years.

continuous_variables.name: Brazilian Legal Amazon annual deforestation (INPE PRODES)
continuous_variables.notes: Verified: 5,796 km2 for the year to July 2025, lowest in 11 years, with Aug 2025-Jan 2026 alerts at 1,325 km2 (lowest six-month reading since 2014). Strongly right-skewed and regime-dependent, NOT a smooth diffusion: the October 2026 Brazilian election is close to a binary fork. Under continued enforcement the series drifts toward 3,000-4,000; under a Bolsonaro-style reversal it jumps to 10,000-13,000 within two years, as it did 2019-2022. Model as a two-state Markov switch with a transition probability tied to the election, not as a single lognormal.

continuous_variables.name: FAO Food Price Index (nominal)
continuous_variables.notes: June 2026 value verified. Right-skewed: food prices grind up and spike down rarely, but spike up violently (2008, 2011, 2022). Drift roughly tracks nominal input-cost inflation. Vol should be regime-switching - roughly 6 index points in normal years and 25+ in shock years. Elevated near-term risk from the El Nino hitting 2027 harvests in South Asia, southern Africa and Australia simultaneously (wheat already forecast -4.3%, rice -1.8%), but note the 2015-16 super El Nino coincided with FALLING food prices, so the ENSO-price link is weaker than intuition suggests.

continuous_variables.name: Annual increase in global 0-2000m ocean heat content
continuous_variables.notes: Verified: 2025 increment was +23 +/- 8 ZJ relative to 2024, the ninth consecutive record year for cumulative OHC. This is the cleanest single measure of Earth's energy imbalance and the least noisy climate metric available - it has increased every year for nine years, so the sign is effectively deterministic even though the magnitude is uncertain. Note the strong anti-correlation with GMST at 1-2 year lag: El Nino years transfer heat from ocean to atmosphere, so expect a lower OHC increment in 2027 alongside a record surface temperature. Do not let the simulation treat these as independently drifting.

feedback_loops.name: Water vapour and lapse-rate feedback
feedback_loops.mechanism: Warmer air holds ~7% more water vapour per degree Celsius (Clausius-Clapeyron); water vapour is the dominant greenhouse gas, roughly doubling the direct CO2 forcing. This is fast, well-constrained, and already embedded in equilibrium climate sensitivity - it should be treated as part of the transfer function from forcing to temperature, not as an additional stochastic loop.

feedback_loops.name: Ice-albedo feedback (Arctic amplification)
feedback_loops.mechanism: Sea ice and snow loss exposes dark ocean and land, cutting surface albedo and increasing absorbed shortwave. The Arctic is warming roughly 3-4x the global rate. The 2026 winter maximum tied the record low, and reduced multi-year ice thickness preconditions faster summer loss. Regionally very strong; globally moderate because the affected area is small.

feedback_loops.name: Clean-technology cost learning curve
feedback_loops.mechanism: Cumulative deployment drives cost declines in solar, wind, batteries and heat pumps (Wright's Law), which drives further deployment. The IEA's verified finding that clean tech deployed since 2019 avoids 3 GtCO2/yr and 35 EJ of annual fossil demand is this loop's output. China's 300+ GW of expected 2026 solar and wind additions and its 21 months of flat-or-falling CO2 are the strongest current evidence. This is the single most powerful balancing force in the system and the main reason emissions have plateaued.

feedback_loops.name: Ocean and land carbon sink uptake
feedback_loops.mechanism: Oceans and terrestrial ecosystems currently absorb roughly half of anthropogenic CO2 emissions, damping atmospheric accumulation. Critically, this loop is weakening: sink efficiency declines as the ocean warms and stratifies, and the land sink is highly variable (near-collapse in 2023, recovery in 2025). Model this as a balancing loop with a slowly declining gain and large interannual noise, because the noise in this term dominates year-to-year CO2 growth variability.

feedback_loops.name: ENSO-carbon-sink coupling
feedback_loops.mechanism: El Nino dries and warms tropical land, suppressing photosynthesis and increasing fire and respiration, which cuts the tropical land carbon sink and raises the atmospheric CO2 growth rate by roughly 1 ppm/yr in strong events. That extra CO2 is permanent while the ENSO warming is transient - so each strong El Nino ratchets the long-term baseline slightly upward. Directly relevant to 2027.

feedback_loops.name: Aerosol unmasking
feedback_loops.mechanism: Sulphate aerosols cool by scattering sunlight and by brightening clouds. Chinese SO2 controls, the IMO 2020 marine fuel sulphur cap and general air-quality improvement remove this cooling, revealing latent greenhouse warming. This is a leading candidate explanation for the unexpected 2023-24 temperature jump. Perversely, successful air-quality policy accelerates warming while saving millions of lives - a genuine and underappreciated policy tension.

feedback_loops.name: Fire-vegetation-carbon loop
feedback_loops.mechanism: Warming and drying increase fire frequency and severity; fires release stored carbon (Canada's 2023 fires alone emitted ~1 GtCO2, and soil/peat carbon is now recognised as the dominant fuel in boreal fires); the released carbon warms further; and post-fire vegetation shifts to lower-carbon states, preventing full recovery. Applies to boreal peat, Amazon and Mediterranean systems. Note H1 2026 saw the lowest global biomass burning emissions on record before a sharp mid-July Canadian escalation - the loop is highly episodic.

feedback_loops.name: Climate damage to political salience to policy
feedback_loops.mechanism: Visible climate disasters raise public concern and can drive policy response. But 2026 demonstrates this loop is weak and can invert: Europe suffered its worst heat mortality event on record in June while the US simultaneously rescinded the endangerment finding and exited Paris. Disaster salience decays within months, and economic pain from mitigation generates a competing backlash loop. Treat the gain as low, noisy, and country-specific rather than as a reliable global stabilizer.

feedback_loops.name: Permafrost carbon feedback
feedback_loops.mechanism: Thawing permafrost releases CO2 and CH4 from ~1,500 GtC of frozen soil carbon, adding forcing that drives further thaw. Real and effectively irreversible on human timescales, but slow: current best estimates put the release at roughly 0.1-0.2 GtC/yr, small against ~10 GtC/yr of fossil emissions. Matters greatly for 2100+ trajectories and very little for a 2036 horizon. Do not let narrative salience inflate its near-term weight in the simulation.

structural_uncertainties: The post-2023 warming acceleration is not fully explained. The 2023-24 jump exceeded CMIP6 expectations and candidate causes - declining planetary albedo from reduced low-cloud cover, aerosol unmasking, Hunga Tonga stratospheric water vapour - have very different implications. If reduced cloud cover is a genuine positive feedback newly engaged, every temperature trajectory here shifts up 0.2-0.4C by 2036 and effective climate sensitivity is higher than assumed. If it was a transient confluence, current anomalies partially relax and the trend reasserts at 0.25C/decade. This single uncertainty dominates the temperature distribution and I cannot resolve it.

Aerosol forcing remains the largest single uncertainty in the total anthropogenic forcing budget, with a range spanning roughly a factor of three. Rapid Asian air-quality improvement plus IMO 2020 could be unmasking substantially more or substantially less warming than models assume. This uncertainty is not independent of the first item - they may be the same phenomenon - and it means near-term warming rate uncertainty is much wider than the smooth drift terms above suggest.

Observational infrastructure is degrading in a way that could break these indicator series. US budget and staffing cuts to NOAA and NASA Earth science, the endangerment finding repeal removing the regulatory rationale for GHG reporting, uncertain continuity for satellite altimetry and gravimetry (GRACE-FO successor), and chronic funding fragility of the RAPID AMOC array all mean several variables here could become unmeasurable or discontinuous before 2031. A simulation that assumes clean observation of these quantities may be forecasting a measurement system that no longer exists.

The models underlying every forecast here largely exclude the nonlinear mechanisms that matter most: marine ice cliff instability, AMOC bistability, Amazon savannization, and abrupt permafrost thaw via thermokarst. Smooth drift-plus-noise formulations are structurally incapable of producing the outcomes with the highest severity scores. Any regime shift in an Earth-system tipping element would invalidate the entire continuous-variable block simultaneously, not one variable at a time.

Carbon sink variability is far larger than models represent. The near-collapse of the terrestrial sink in 2023 followed by a reported recovery in 2025 shows swings of several GtC/yr with no corresponding change in emissions. If the sink weakens durably - through tropical drought, fire, or ocean stratification - atmospheric CO2 growth could jump by 1-2 ppm/yr while emissions are flat or falling, decoupling the emissions indicator from the concentration indicator that actually drives warming. Most policy models implicitly assume a stable sink fraction.

Solar radiation management is a wildcard that decouples temperature from emissions on a 2-5 year timescale. A unilateral deployment would break every relationship in this model, and the subsequent termination-shock risk is an entirely new hazard class with no historical analogue. The probabilities I assign are near-pure judgement with essentially no reference class - capability is proliferating faster than governance and my confidence is genuinely low in both directions.

Threshold definitions are institutional choices, not physical facts. Whether '1.5C is breached' depends on the baseline period, the dataset (ERA5, GISTEMP, HadCRUT and Berkeley Earth differ by up to 0.1C), whether the metric is a single year, a 20-year centred mean, or estimated human-induced warming, and whether an institution chooses to declare at all. Several risks here could resolve differently under equally defensible definitions without any change in the physical world. Consumers of this model should not mistake definitional resolution for physical resolution.

The emissions pathway is dominated by a small number of political decisions rather than smooth technology diffusion: China's 15th Five-Year Plan carbon intensity target, the October 2026 Brazilian election's effect on Amazon land use, the 2028 US election's effect on Paris re-entry and the endangerment finding, and India's post-2030 coal trajectory. These are lumpy, correlated, and poorly modelled as stochastic drift. A simulation treating emissions as a diffusion process will systematically understate both the upside and downside tails.

(1) AI: the five largest hyperscalers are on track for ~$725bn of 2026 capex vs ~$412bn in 2025; Morgan Stanley expects ~$570bn of AI-related debt issuance in 2026 (~$236bn done by 31 May), with roughly $800bn of data-center financing migrating into private credit and off-balance-sheet structures. The Nasdaq flirted with correction in mid-late July on capex-funding doubts and reports of a Chinese chipmaking breakthrough. (2) Private credit: Fitch's broad measure put the true US default rate at 5.8% for the 12 months to Jan 2026; the FSB published a vulnerabilities report on 6 May; Blackstone's BCRED took $6.5bn of redemption requests (7.9%) in Q1. Office CMBS delinquency hit 12.34% in Jan, above the GFC peak, with ~$930bn of CRE debt maturing in 2026. (3) Sovereigns: CBO puts the FY2026 US deficit near $1.9trn, debt held by the public at ~100% of GDP, interest above $1trn; the 10-year exceeded 4.6% in late July, 45bp above CBO's assumption. IIF has global debt at ~$353trn in Q1 2026. USD share of allocated reserves has fallen below 57%. China grew 4.3% y/y in Q2 (weakest since Q4 2022), with property investment -18% y/y in H1 and a tenth consecutive quarter of deflation.
