discrete_risks.name: Global recession (world real GDP growth below 2.0% in a calendar year)
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: IMF WEO (October vintage of the following year) reports world real GDP growth at market or PPP weights below 2.0% for any calendar year in the window. Resolves YES on the first such year.
discrete_risks.reasoning: IMF has 2026 at 3.0% with two quarters largely banked, so 2026 is effectively off the table; the risk starts with 2027. The distinctive feature of this cycle is that a large energy supply shock and a large AI investment boom are partially cancelling. If the AI capex impulse stalls while oil stays above $90, the offset disappears and global growth drops fast — hyperscaler capex alone is ~0.6-0.7% of world GDP in flow terms.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: calendar years 1980-2025 (46 years). Sub-2% world growth occurred in 1982, 1991, 2009 and 2020, with 1981 borderline — 4-5 events, ~9-10% per year. Clustering means conditional probabilities are not independent.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: The AI capex cycle may be far more durable than the bubble narrative suggests, and unlike telecom in 2000 it is being funded substantially from operating cash flow of firms with 30%+ margins. Global growth has now absorbed COVID, a European energy war, a 500bp hiking cycle and a Hormuz shock without going sub-2%. The world economy is measurably less oil-intensive per unit of GDP than in any prior shock, and services trade is still growing near 5%. I may be over-weighting fragility that has repeatedly failed to bite.

discrete_risks.name: US recession with NBER-dated peak in the window
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee assigns a business-cycle peak dated between August 2026 and the end of the stated year. Later announcement is fine; the peak date is what counts.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Payrolls at +57k in June with 74k of downward revisions, participation down 0.3pp, and unemployment falling only because the labour force shrank — that is a labour market at stall speed. Against that: the Fed is being pushed toward hiking by a 4.7% global inflation print and an energy shock, which is the classic recession-generating configuration. Prediction markets have end-2026 recession odds in the low teens (down from 39% on Kalshi in March), which I read as correct for 2026 and too sanguine for 2027.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: NBER-dated US recessions 1945-2025 — 12 peaks in 80 years, ~15% unconditional annual onset probability. Over a 17-month window that implies ~21% baseline; over 5.4 years ~58%; over 10.4 years ~82%.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Household and corporate balance sheets are in far better shape than pre-2008, fiscal policy is running a 6%-of-GDP deficit that is inherently countercyclical, and the AI capex wave gives the investment component of GDP an unusually rate-insensitive floor. Weak payrolls in a labour market with collapsing immigration-driven labour supply may signal a lower breakeven job growth rate, not weakening demand — 57k could be full employment now.

discrete_risks.name: AI capex bust: aggregate hyperscaler capex falls 20%+ year over year
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: Combined calendar-year capital expenditure of Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle, as reported in audited annual filings, comes in at least 20% below the prior calendar year's reported total, for any year in the window.
discrete_risks.reasoning: 2026 capex of ~$725bn is up ~76% on 2025 and 2027 commitments are largely contracted, so a 2027 print 20% below 2026 is near-impossible mechanically — land, power contracts and chip allocations are pre-committed. The real risk window is 2028-2031, when either depreciation catches up with AI revenue or credit markets refuse to fund the next leg. Morgan Stanley's ~$570bn of 2026 AI debt issuance, with roughly $800bn of data-center financing in private/off-balance-sheet vehicles, is the transmission channel: the marginal dollar is now borrowed, and borrowed dollars stop abruptly.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: post-boom capex collapses in capital-intensive tech. US telecom capex fell roughly 30-50% peak-to-trough 2001-2003; semiconductor equipment capex has fallen 20%+ y/y in 1996, 1998, 2001, 2009, 2019 and 2023 — roughly six times in thirty years for that narrower series, ~20%/yr in a cyclical industry, but hyperscaler capex has never fallen year over year in its history.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Inference demand, not training, may become the dominant load, and inference spend scales with revenue rather than with speculative capability bets — that makes capex self-funding and much less bust-prone. Hyperscalers also have the option to slow growth to zero rather than cut, which is what they did in 2022-23; a 20% absolute decline requires actual asset abandonment. Note the July 2026 selloff was partly driven by reports of a Chinese chipmaking breakthrough, which would lower unit costs and could raise physical buildout while lowering dollar capex — an outcome my resolution criterion would misread.

discrete_risks.name: S&P 500 falls 30%+ from its all-time closing high
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: S&P 500 records a daily close at least 30% below its prior all-time closing high, at any point in the window.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Shiller CAPE at 40.9 is the second-highest reading in 155 years and the cyclically adjusted earnings yield is ~2.4% against a 4.6% ten-year — the equity risk premium is negative. Top-10 concentration at ~40% means index-level drawdown risk is really idiosyncratic risk in five to ten AI-linked names. Valuation is a terrible timing tool but a decent conditional-severity tool: it does not raise the probability of a downturn much, it raises the probability that a downturn is deep.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: S&P 500 30%+ drawdowns since 1950 — 1968-70, 1973-74, 1987, 2000-02, 2007-09, 2020. Six episodes in 76 years, ~8% annual onset. Conditioning on a starting CAPE above 30 (only 1929, 1999-2000, 2021, 2024-26), the base rate is materially higher but the sample is four.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: The index's earnings base is now dominated by asset-light, high-margin, net-cash businesses whose fair multiple genuinely is higher than the 20th-century average; CAPE's ten-year trailing earnings window also mechanically penalises a period containing the 2020 earnings hole. Mag-7 has already underperformed the index by 7% year to date without an index-level bear market, which is exactly how concentration risk resolves benignly — through rotation, not collapse.

discrete_risks.name: Brent crude settles above $120/bbl
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: ICE Brent front-month futures settle at or above $120.00/bbl on any trading day in the window.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Brent already touched $118 on 29 April 2026 without full Hormuz closure, so the distance to the threshold is small and the conflict is unresolved — prices re-spiked from $72 in late June to $94 in mid-July. The 2027 window therefore carries most of the cumulative probability; conditional on the Iran conflict being frozen or settled by 2028, the structural picture (OPEC+ spare capacity, slowing Chinese oil demand, EV penetration) is bearish, which is why my increments after 2027 are modest.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: Brent above $120 nominal occurred in 2008, 2011-2013 (sustained) and 2022 — roughly four distinct episodes in the last twenty years, ~15-20% per year unconditionally, but heavily conditional on Middle East supply disruption, which is currently active.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: The 2026 shock is the strongest evidence yet that the oil market absorbs disruption faster than anyone models: a ~10 mb/d initial disruption produced a peak of $118, not $200, and the price was back at $72 within two months. US shale, strategic reserves, OPEC+ spare capacity and demand destruction now form a wide, fast-acting buffer. Also note that $120 in 2036 dollars is a much lower real price than $120 today, which pushes the later-window probability up for purely nominal reasons — an argument my numbers may under-weight.

discrete_risks.name: Sustained effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: Seaborne crude and condensate transits through the Strait of Hormuz fall more than 50% below the 2025 monthly average for at least 14 consecutive days, per IEA, EIA, Kpler or Vortexa reporting, at any point from August 2026 onward.
discrete_risks.reasoning: A live shooting war involving Iran has produced attacks on shipping and energy infrastructure but not, so far, a sustained 50%+ transit collapse; Iran's own export dependence and Chinese pressure both cut against full closure. That structural logic has held for four decades including the Tanker War. Most of the probability mass is in 2026-2027 while the conflict is hot; after a settlement the hazard rate drops sharply.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: the Strait has never been closed for a sustained period despite the 1980-88 Tanker War, the 2019 tanker attacks, the 2020 Soleimani strike and the 2024-26 escalations — zero events in roughly 45 years of periodic threat, which is the single most important calibration fact here.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: The base rate of zero is exactly what you would expect from a regime that had never faced existential decapitation. The February 2026 campaign explicitly targeted Iranian leadership and command centres; a regime that concludes it is being destroyed anyway has no reason to preserve its own export revenue. Conversely, the risk may already be lower than I say — if the June ceasefire holds and Iran's naval and missile capacity was substantially degraded, the physical ability to close the strait may no longer exist.

discrete_risks.name: US 10-year Treasury yield closes at or above 6.00%
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: The constant-maturity 10-year US Treasury yield (H.15 / Treasury daily par yield curve) closes at or above 6.00% on any day in the window.
discrete_risks.reasoning: The 10-year has just cleared 4.6%, 45bp above CBO's assumption, with a $1.9trn deficit, >$1trn of interest and a Fed that may be hiking rather than cutting. Getting to 6% requires roughly 140bp more, which realistically needs either sustained 4-5% inflation or a genuine term-premium repricing of US fiscal credibility. Neither is central, both are live. CRFB estimates each sustained 0.1pp adds ~$379bn to a decade of interest cost, so this is the single highest-leverage macro variable in the model.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: the 10-year has been above 6% in roughly 27 of the 63 years since 1962, but not once since 2000 — the regime matters more than the unconditional frequency. Since 2000: zero occurrences in 26 years. The relevant question is regime-change probability, not tail frequency within the current regime.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Structural demand for duration — pension and insurance liability matching, stablecoin issuers now forced by the GENIUS Act into T-bills and short Treasuries, and the sheer absence of substitutes — puts a firm ceiling on US yields. Every 'bond vigilante' episode since 1994 has ended with yields lower a year later. Japan runs 236.7% debt/GDP with a 10-year near 2%; the notion that 100% debt/GDP forces 6% yields is not supported by cross-country evidence.

discrete_risks.name: US CPI inflation returns to 5.0%+ year over year
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: BLS reports headline CPI-U at or above 5.0% year over year for any single month in the window.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Headline is 3.5% with energy contributing +15.7% y/y and core at only 2.6%, so the gap to 5% is essentially one more oil spike. The IMF explicitly says global disinflation has stalled and revised world inflation up to 4.7%. Offsetting: the Section 122 surcharge just expired and the effective tariff rate has fallen from ~14.9% to ~7.2%, which is a genuine disinflationary impulse into H2 2026, and core at 2.6% means expectations look anchored.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: US CPI above 5% y/y in any month — occurred in 1969-71, 1973-75, 1978-82, 1990 (briefly), 2008 (briefly) and 2021-23. Roughly six episodes in 58 years, ~10%/yr unconditionally, but strongly conditional on oil shocks, and one is in progress.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: The 2021-23 episode showed that supply-driven inflation unwinds fast once the shock passes; June's -0.4% m/m print was the largest monthly decline since April 2020, driven entirely by the ceasefire. Core at 2.6% and falling suggests no second-round wage effects at all, and a labour market adding 57k jobs will not generate them. A new Fed chair with hawkish credentials arguably lowers this risk further.

discrete_risks.name: Japan 10-year government bond yield reaches 3.00%
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: The 10-year JGB benchmark yield closes at or above 3.00% on any day in the window.
discrete_risks.reasoning: This is the most under-priced global duration risk. The 10-year cleared 2% in December 2025, the 40-year broke 4% in January, the BOJ is at 1.00% and 86% of economists expect 1.25% by December, the yen is at a 40-year low forcing further tightening, and PM Takaichi is running expansionary fiscal policy against 236.7% debt/GDP. The 30-year is already at all-time highs. Getting the 10-year from ~2% to 3% requires only a continuation of the trend already in place.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: the 10-year JGB has not been at 3% since 1994 — zero occurrences in 32 years. But that entire period was one of deflation and yield-curve control, both of which have now ended; the base rate is drawn from a regime that no longer exists, which is precisely when base rates mislead.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Japan's domestic institutional base — life insurers, banks, GPIF, and the BOJ still holding roughly half of outstanding JGBs — provides captive demand that no other sovereign enjoys, and the BOJ retains the ability to cap yields if it chooses. A move to 3% would also trigger such a violent yen appreciation and carry-trade unwind that Japanese authorities would intervene long before. Every prior 'JGB widowmaker' trade has lost money for thirty years.

discrete_risks.name: France or Italy 10-year spread over Bunds exceeds 300bp
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: The 10-year OAT-Bund or BTP-Bund spread closes above 300 basis points for five consecutive trading days, or the ECB formally activates the Transmission Protection Instrument for either sovereign.
discrete_risks.reasoning: The notable H1 2026 development is that the French 30-year yield crossed above the Italian despite France's lower debt ratio (~115% vs ~135%) — a credibility, not arithmetic, judgment, with the French 30-year at 4.5%, the highest since 2009. France's chronic inability to legislate a budget is the mechanism. But 300bp is a genuine crisis level, roughly triple current spreads, and the TPI's existence is designed to make it unreachable. NOT VERIFIED: I could not confirm current spread levels this session.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: euro-area 10-year spreads above 300bp — Italy in 2011-12 and briefly 2018; Spain, Portugal, Ireland, Greece in 2010-12. Since the 2012 'whatever it takes' commitment and the 2022 creation of the TPI: one near-miss (Italy 2018, ~330bp intraday) in 14 years.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: The ECB's reaction function is now explicit and unlimited in principle; conditional on TPI eligibility, spreads simply cannot reach 300bp because the ECB has committed to preventing it, and markets know this. The counter-counter-argument is that TPI eligibility requires compliance with EU fiscal rules — precisely what France is failing at — so the backstop may be legally unavailable to the country that needs it, which is why I hold the 2031 number at 20% rather than lower.

discrete_risks.name: Large private-credit vehicle suspends redemptions or enters wind-down
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: A private credit fund, BDC or interval fund with at least $20bn NAV fully suspends redemptions (beyond pro-rating within stated quarterly limits) for at least one month, or is placed into wind-down or forced sale, in the US, UK or EU.
discrete_risks.reasoning: The precursors are all present: Fitch's broad measure has US private credit defaults at 5.8% with 60% of those involving PIK or interest deferral (i.e., the true number is worse than the headline), Blackstone's BCRED absorbed $6.5bn of redemption requests in Q1 2026, the FSB published a formal vulnerabilities report on 6 May, and the BIS named AI-related private credit as one of three top systemic risks. Semi-liquid vehicles holding illiquid assets have a well-understood failure mode. Note the resolution bar is deliberately high — pro-rating within stated limits is normal design and does not count.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: open-ended funds holding illiquid assets that gated — UK property funds 2016 and 2020 (multiple, several £2-4bn), Woodford 2019, H2O 2020, US non-traded REITs 2022-23 (BREIT pro-rated but never suspended). Roughly one significant gating cluster every 4-5 years, though a full suspension at $20bn+ scale in credit specifically has not yet happened.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Private credit's structure is genuinely more run-resistant than the 2008 shadow-banking analogy suggests: capital is largely locked in closed-end drawdown funds, semi-liquid vehicles have hard quarterly caps that worked as designed in Q1 2026, and mark-to-model actually suppresses the fire-sale dynamic rather than amplifying it. Losses may be large and slow rather than sudden — a decade of poor returns for LPs, not a systemic event. Rising defaults with PIK conversion is precisely the mechanism by which stress is absorbed without a run.

discrete_risks.name: Failure or extraordinary rescue of a bank with over $250bn in assets
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: A bank holding company with more than $250bn in total assets in the US, EU, UK, Switzerland, Japan or China fails, is placed into resolution, is forced into a state-brokered merger, or receives an extraordinary government capital injection or central bank emergency liquidity facility created specifically for it.
discrete_risks.reasoning: The mechanism would be CRE rather than AI: office CMBS delinquency at 12.34% is a record and above the GFC peak, ~$930bn of CRE debt matures in 2026, and 1,788 US banks hold CRE above 300% of equity. But that concentration is overwhelmingly in banks well below $250bn — the large institutions largely avoided this cycle's CRE exposure. The over-$250bn threshold makes this a genuinely rare event. Bank-to-private-credit lending, flagged by the FSB, is the channel by which small-bank stress could reach a large one.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: banks over $250bn (inflation-adjusted) failing or rescued in advanced economies — 2008 (Bear, Lehman, WaMu, Wachovia, RBS, Fortis, Dexia, Citi/BofA support) and 2023 (Credit Suisse, and First Republic at ~$230bn just under). Two clusters in 20 years, so roughly 10% per year unconditionally but with extreme clustering — most years are zero.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Post-2023 large banks hold materially more capital and HQLA than at any point in modern history, and the 2023 episode demonstrated that authorities will now act within a weekend to prevent a headline failure — which means the event resolves as 'extraordinary rescue' rather than 'failure', and my criterion captures that. Conversely I may be too high: CRE losses are being realised slowly through extend-and-pretend, and slow losses do not kill banks, they just depress ROE.

discrete_risks.name: China reports annual real GDP growth below 4.0%
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: China's National Bureau of Statistics reports full-year real GDP growth below 4.0% for any calendar year in the window, in the initial annual release.
discrete_risks.reasoning: Q2 2026 printed 4.3%, the weakest since Q4 2022, with property investment down 18% y/y, fixed asset investment down 5.7% ytd (worst since May 2020) and a tenth consecutive quarter of deflation. Growth is being held up by AI-related exports, which is a fragile single pillar given tariff and export-control risk. 2026 full-year probably still lands near 4.5-4.8%; 2027 is the first real test. Beyond 2028, demographics and the exhaustion of the property/land-finance model make sub-4% the modal path.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: NBS-reported annual growth below 4% since 1991 — only 2020 (2.2%) and 2022 (3.0%). Two in 35 years. But the reported series is heavily managed toward the announced target, so the relevant base rate is 'how often has Beijing accepted publishing a sub-4 number', not 'how often did the economy grow below 4%'.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: The number is a policy output as much as an economic one; Beijing has consistently delivered prints within 0.3pp of target and has abundant statistical and fiscal levers to keep doing so. Real activity may already be well below 4% without the reported figure ever going there — which means my criterion could resolve NO even as the underlying risk fully materialises. This is a measurement-validity problem, not a forecasting one.

discrete_risks.name: China announces a central-government property/LGFV rescue of RMB 5trn or more
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: China's State Council, MOF or PBOC announces a single package of central-government fiscal support, debt assumption or recapitalization directed at the property sector and/or local government financing vehicles totalling at least RMB 5 trillion, announced as one program.
discrete_risks.reasoning: The 2024 package was RMB 6trn over three years, i.e. RMB 2trn per year, and expires at end-2026 — that alone creates a decision point. LGFV debt is roughly 50% of GDP versus 30% for official local debt, and land sale revenue has collapsed with property investment down 18%. Beijing's revealed preference has been incrementalism ('extend and pretend'), which argues against a single mega-package; but the end of the current swap program plus a possible sub-4% growth print is the scenario that forces one.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: Chinese single-announcement stimulus at 4%+ of GDP — the 2008 RMB 4trn package (~12% of GDP then) and the 2024 RMB 6trn debt swap (~4.5% of GDP). Two in 18 years, roughly 11% per year, though both followed acute stress.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Xi's ideological commitment to avoiding 'welfarism' and moral hazard in property has been remarkably durable across four years of deterioration, and the leadership genuinely appears to prefer a controlled deflationary grind that reallocates capital to manufacturing and AI. There is also a real chance a large package happens but is structured as multiple announcements below my RMB 5trn single-package bar — a definitional false negative.

discrete_risks.name: US average effective tariff rate exceeds 15%
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: Penn Wharton Budget Model or Yale Budget Lab reports a US average effective tariff rate on all imports above 15.0% for at least one full month in the window.
discrete_risks.reasoning: The rate peaked near 14.9% and has fallen to ~7.2% and lower after the Supreme Court struck IEEPA (20 Feb) and Section 122 expired (24 July). The administration is visibly rebuilding on Section 232 (steel/aluminium/copper overhauled 6 April, pharma effective 31 July, medtech under investigation) plus Sections 301 and 338 — but 232 requires sector-by-sector investigations, which is inherently slower and narrower than a blanket IEEPA power. Getting back above 15% requires either a large number of completed 232 actions or Congressional grant of blanket authority. The November midterms are the key branch point.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: US average effective tariff rate above 15% — last sustained in the 1930s (Smoot-Hawley era) until 2025. One occurrence in 90 years before 2025, and one in 2025-26. The regime has already broken once, so historical rarity is weak evidence.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: The Supreme Court ruling is a durable structural constraint, not a speed bump: 6-3 majorities on major-questions grounds do not get worked around quickly, and Section 232's national-security predicate cannot plausibly cover all imports. Courts may also narrow 232 next. Meanwhile the political salience of tariff-driven consumer prices, with headline CPI at 3.5%, cuts against re-escalation ahead of midterms. There is a symmetric risk my number is too low if Congress flips and grants explicit authority.

discrete_risks.name: Major stablecoin failure or sustained depeg
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: A stablecoin with at least $20bn market capitalization trades more than 5% below its peg for more than 24 consecutive hours, or its issuer suspends or fails to honor redemptions for more than 24 hours.
discrete_risks.reasoning: The sector is now ~$320bn with GENIUS Act final rules landing July 2026 and enforcement from January 2027, requiring 100% backing in dollars or short T-bills. Full reserve backing in the safest asset in the world materially lowers depeg risk relative to the 2022 environment — issuers bought ~$109bn of T-bills to comply. The residual risk is offshore or partially-compliant issuers, and the operational risk of a redemption gate during a T-bill market disruption. Note the linkage now runs both ways: a stablecoin run would be a forced seller into the T-bill market.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: stablecoins above $20bn that broke — TerraUSD (May 2022, ~$18bn at peak, total loss) and USDC (March 2023, depegged ~12% over a weekend on SVB exposure, recovered inside 72 hours, ~$40bn). Two events in roughly six years of the asset class existing at that scale, but under a pre-regulatory regime.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: Full T-bill backing under a federal statute makes this closer to a money market fund than to Terra, and MMFs broke the buck twice in 50 years. The genuine contrarian worry runs the other way: regulation may have concentrated the sector into two or three issuers whose failure would be systemically much larger, and the systemic damage would flow through the Treasury market, not through crypto. Severity might be materially higher than 4 by 2031.

discrete_risks.name: Wave of emerging-market sovereign defaults or restructurings
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: At least three additional sovereigns, each with more than $10bn in external public debt, default on external commercial debt or formally enter a comprehensive debt restructuring or a new IMF Extended Fund Facility of at least $3bn, between August 2026 and the end of the stated year.
discrete_risks.reasoning: IMF credit outstanding is at ~SDR 110bn, the highest in the Fund's 80-year history. OECD flags 2026-2027 as the peak years for LMIC refinancing with interest-rate differentials near five percentage points, and the 10-year UST at 4.6%+ sets the floor for everything. Argentina alone carries $60bn of IMF debt. Against that: EM external balance sheets are structurally better than in prior cycles — more local-currency issuance, larger reserve buffers, and commodity exporters are benefiting from the oil and critical-minerals price surge.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: EM sovereign default/restructuring clusters — 1982-89 (Latin America, 20+ sovereigns), 1997-2002 (Asia, Russia, Argentina, ~10), 2020-24 (Zambia, Sri Lanka, Ghana, Lebanon, Ethiopia, Suriname, ~6). Roughly three clusters in 45 years; three qualifying events inside a given ~17-month window is uncommon but not rare.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: High oil and metals prices are a massive terms-of-trade windfall for a large share of the distressed universe, and Argentina is preparing a return to international markets after eight years — that is the opposite of a default wave. The IMF's own lending capacity and the G20 Common Framework, however creaky, have so far prevented disorderly outcomes. My $10bn/$3bn thresholds also exclude the small frontier sovereigns where most actual defaults occur, biasing toward NO.

discrete_risks.name: US dollar share of allocated FX reserves falls below 50%
discrete_risks.resolution_criteria: IMF COFER reports the US dollar share of allocated global foreign exchange reserves below 50.0% for any quarter in the window.
discrete_risks.reasoning: The share fell below 57% for the first time since 1995 (56.9% in Q3 2025) and continues to decline, and central bank gold holdings (~$5.2trn) now exceed foreign official holdings of US Treasuries — a genuine milestone. But the decline is roughly 1pp per year and substantially driven by valuation effects (gold price appreciation) rather than active dollar selling. Getting to 50% requires ~7pp, i.e. seven years at the current pace with no reversal; 2031 is therefore right at the boundary and 2036 is more likely than not on trend, which is why I put 38% rather than higher — trend extrapolation over a decade deserves heavy discounting.
discrete_risks.base_rate_anchor: Reference class: the dollar's reserve share fell from 72% (2001) to ~57% (2025) — 15pp in 24 years, ~0.6pp/yr average, with the pace accelerating to roughly 1pp/yr recently. Sterling's displacement took roughly three decades after the underlying economic crossover.
discrete_risks.contrarian_case: No alternative currency offers the dollar's liquidity, depth or network effects; the euro lacks a unified safe asset, the renminbi is capital-controlled, and gold is a store of value but not a payment or funding currency. The 'other currencies' bucket is fragmenting across AUD, CAD, KRW and CNY rather than consolidating, which slows displacement. Much of the observed decline is arithmetic — gold appreciation inflating the denominator — and would reverse on a gold correction. Note also that reserve share and dollar dominance in trade invoicing and funding are different things, and the latter has barely moved.

continuous_variables.name: Brent crude oil price
continuous_variables.notes: Log-normal is the better generator; 25 $/bbl at an $84 level is roughly 30% annualized relative vol, consistent with historical Brent. Fat right tail from Hormuz. The 2026 range alone was $72-118. Long-run drift slightly negative in real terms from EV penetration and Chinese demand plateau, offset by nominal inflation.

continuous_variables.name: US 10-year Treasury yield
continuous_variables.notes: Mean-reverting around a rising anchor: CBO baseline pushes net interest to 4.6% of GDP by 2036, which mechanically raises the equilibrium term premium. Random-walk scaling would give a wider band than shown; the deciles embed partial mean reversion. Verified starting point: closed above 4.6% on 21 July 2026, 45bp above CBO's 4.1% assumption.

continuous_variables.name: US CPI inflation, year over year
continuous_variables.notes: Strongly mean-reverting to roughly 2.5% under a credible Fed; the current level is energy-driven (energy +15.7% y/y) while core sits at 2.6%. Vol should be treated as shock-driven with heavy positive skew tied to the oil variable — correlate this node with brent_crude at roughly +0.4.

continuous_variables.name: Federal funds target rate, upper bound
continuous_variables.notes: Near-term risk is skewed UP (futures price ~4% by end-2026 on energy inflation), medium-term skewed DOWN (recession cuts). Regime uncertainty is unusually high: Warsh took office 22 May 2026 with no observed reaction function as chair. Should be modelled as a jump process, not diffusion — the Fed moves in 25bp steps and cuts far faster than it hikes.

continuous_variables.name: S&P 500 index level
continuous_variables.notes: Deciles derived from geometric drift ~6.5%/yr and ~17-18% annualized vol, compounding on the level rather than the stated linear drift. Starting CAPE of 40.9 argues for below-average forward returns, so the median implies multiple compression against earnings growth. Left tail is fatter than lognormal given ~40% top-10 concentration.

continuous_variables.name: Global real GDP growth
continuous_variables.notes: Distribution is left-skewed: the upside is bounded by capacity (~4.5% is a boom ceiling) while the downside is unbounded in a shock year (2020 was -3%). Verified anchor: IMF July 2026 WEO Update, 3.0% for 2026 and 3.4% for 2027. Should be driven by, not independent of, the oil, US recession and AI capex nodes.

continuous_variables.name: China reported real GDP growth
continuous_variables.notes: Reported series is policy-smoothed: realised vol of the official print is far lower than underlying activity vol, so vol here should be low with occasional downward level shifts when targets are reset. Q2 2026 came in at 4.3%, the weakest since Q4 2022. Demographics plus the exhaustion of land finance imply a persistent negative drift regardless of stimulus.

continuous_variables.name: US federal debt held by the public / GDP
continuous_variables.notes: CBO baseline is ~120% by 2036, or ~125% if current elevated rates persist. Vol is low because the accumulation is mechanical; the real uncertainty is a step-change from a recession (automatic stabilizers plus a fiscal response add 8-12pp in one to two years), so model as low diffusion plus a jump conditioned on the US recession node.

continuous_variables.name: USD share of allocated FX reserves (IMF COFER)
continuous_variables.notes: Verified: fell below 57% for the first time since 1995 (56.9%, Q3 2025). A large part of the observed decline is valuation-driven (gold appreciation inflating the denominator), so this node should be negatively correlated with the gold node — a gold correction would partially reverse the measured decline without any change in behaviour.

continuous_variables.name: Gold price
continuous_variables.notes: Verified at roughly $4,040/oz on 29 July 2026. NOT VERIFIED: a widely repeated claim of a $5,542/oz January 2026 record, which I judge unreliable and have excluded. Central banks have bought over 1,000 tonnes a year for four consecutive years and official gold holdings (~$5.2trn) now exceed foreign official Treasury holdings — a structural bid independent of real rates.

continuous_variables.name: USD/JPY exchange rate
continuous_variables.notes: At a 40-year low after ¥11.73trn of MoF intervention in April-May 2026. Drift is modestly toward yen appreciation as the BOJ normalizes from 1.00% while the Fed eventually eases, but carry dynamics can overshoot violently in both directions. This node should be tightly coupled to the JGB yield risk — a 3% 10-year JGB implies a disorderly carry unwind and a sharp move below 130.

continuous_variables.name: US average effective tariff rate on all imports
continuous_variables.notes: Verified 7.2% in May 2026 per Penn Wharton; current value estimated near 6% after Section 122 expired 24 July, though the post-expiry figure is NOT VERIFIED. Highly discontinuous and policy-driven: model as a jump process conditioned on the Nov 2026 midterms, Section 232 completions and further court rulings, not as a diffusion.

feedback_loops.name: AI capex wealth loop
feedback_loops.mechanism: Hyperscaler capex ($725bn in 2026, up from $412bn) becomes semiconductor and infrastructure revenue, which lifts earnings for a top-10 cohort that is ~40% of the S&P 500, which lifts equity wealth and lowers the cost of capital, which validates and finances the next capex round — increasingly via debt (~$570bn of AI-related issuance in 2026). The loop runs in reverse with the same gearing: a capex pause cuts semiconductor earnings, hits a concentrated index, raises the cost of the debt already issued, and forces further capex cuts.

feedback_loops.name: Sovereign debt-service doom loop
feedback_loops.mechanism: Higher yields raise interest outlays (US already above $1trn, ~3.3% of GDP), which widen deficits, which increase issuance, which raises the term premium, which raises yields. CRFB estimates each sustained 0.1pp adds ~$379bn over a decade. The loop is currently live in the US, France and Japan simultaneously — the first time three major sovereigns have been in it at once since the 1980s.

feedback_loops.name: Oil shock demand destruction
feedback_loops.mechanism: An energy price spike raises headline inflation (global inflation revised up to 4.7%), which forces central banks to tighten (ECB hiked in June, Fed on hold with hikes priced), which destroys demand and cuts oil consumption, which brings the price back down. Visible in 2026: Brent $118 in April to $72 in June. It is the mechanism by which supply shocks self-correct, at the cost of output.

feedback_loops.name: Private credit mark-to-model unravelling
feedback_loops.mechanism: Rising defaults (5.8% on Fitch's broad measure, 60% via PIK or deferral) trigger redemption requests ($6.5bn at BCRED in Q1), which force asset sales, which establish observable marks below carrying value, which trigger further redemptions and force bank lenders to the funds to pull lines. Layered leverage — company, fund, bank, CLO — amplifies each turn.

feedback_loops.name: China property-land-LGFV deflation spiral
feedback_loops.mechanism: Falling property investment (-18% y/y in H1 2026) collapses land sale revenue, starving local governments and LGFVs (~50% of GDP in debt) of cash, forcing spending cuts and asset sales that further depress land and property prices, deepening deflation (ten consecutive quarters) which raises real debt burdens. Each round requires larger central-government transfers to arrest.

feedback_loops.name: Dollar-EM funding loop
feedback_loops.mechanism: Risk-off drives dollar demand; a stronger dollar raises the local-currency cost of EM external debt service just as the 10-year UST sits above 4.6%, forcing EM fiscal tightening and reserve drawdown; weaker EM demand slows global growth, which drives further risk-off and dollar demand. Currently attenuated by high commodity prices helping EM exporters.

feedback_loops.name: Passive concentration flywheel
feedback_loops.mechanism: Index-tracking flows are allocated by market capitalization, so the largest names receive the largest inflows, which raises their weight, which directs still more of the next dollar to them. The Mag-7 at 32.5% and top-10 at ~40% of the index means index investors are involuntarily concentrated. Unwinds symmetrically and violently on outflow.

feedback_loops.name: Tariff-inflation-political feedback
feedback_loops.mechanism: Tariffs raise import prices and headline inflation, which is politically salient, which raises the electoral cost of tariffs and generates legal and legislative pushback — visible in the Supreme Court's 20 February 2026 IEEPA ruling and the lapse of the Section 122 surcharge. The effective rate fell from ~14.9% to ~7.2%. The balancing force is real but slow and can be overridden by security framing under Section 232.

feedback_loops.name: Central bank credibility anchor
feedback_loops.mechanism: So long as long-run inflation expectations stay anchored, a supply shock raises headline inflation without triggering second-round wage effects — US core at 2.6% versus headline 3.5% is the anchor working. The loop is nonlinear: it holds until it does not, and the anchor's strength is being tested by a new Fed chair, fiscal dominance pressures and a second consecutive energy shock within four years.

structural_uncertainties: AI as a genuine total factor productivity shock. If AI raises trend productivity growth by even 0.5-1.0pp, then debt/GDP paths, equity valuations at CAPE 40.9, and the sustainability of a 4.6% 10-year all look completely different — the denominator grows out of the problem, and what looks like a bubble is a correctly-priced regime change. Every risk in this model that is anchored on debt sustainability or valuation reversion is conditionally wrong in that world. Conversely, if AI capex proves to be a depreciating expense rather than a productive asset, the same nodes are far too optimistic. I have no reliable way to distinguish these ex ante and the model should be run under both regimes.

Measurement validity is deteriorating exactly where it matters most. Private credit assets are marked to model with no observable prices; Fitch found 60% of defaults hidden inside PIK conversions and interest deferrals. Chinese official GDP is policy-smoothed to the point where the reported series may resolve NO on my sub-4% criterion while activity is well below it. GDP treatment of AI capex — capitalization boundaries, useful-life assumptions on GPUs, and whether circular vendor-financed revenue is double-counted — could be overstating measured growth by a non-trivial margin. Several of my indicators may be measuring the wrong thing.

Fed reaction-function regime break. Kevin Warsh took office on 22 May 2026 with no observable record as chair and a historical preference for a smaller balance sheet and rules-based policy, appointed after the most divisive confirmation vote in Fed history. Any econometric relationship between inflation, unemployment and policy rates estimated on 1994-2025 data may simply not apply. The tail case — political pressure producing fiscal dominance, with inflation used deliberately to erode a 100%-of-GDP debt stock — would invert the sign on real rates, the dollar and gold simultaneously and is not representable in my continuous variables.

Geopolitics is now the dominant generator and it sits outside this domain. The single largest macro event of H1 2026 was a war, not a financial development. A Taiwan contingency — with over 90% of advanced chips still made there and no volume sub-5nm production outside Taiwan before 2027 — would make every variable in this model second-order within days. The financial system's response to a genuine loss of leading-edge semiconductor supply has no historical analogue and no reliable prior.

The 2025-26 shock sequence suggests the shock generator is not in any historical dataset. A supreme court invalidating a president's tariff authority, a 150-day statutory surcharge, a joint strike campaign on Iran producing the largest oil supply disruption on record, and a Fed chair replacement all happened inside eighteen months. Consensus forecasts and prediction markets were badly miscalibrated on each. My base rates are drawn from a period of institutional stability that may have ended, which biases every 'rare event' probability in this model downward.

Physical constraints may bind before financial ones. Electricity generation, transformer and turbine lead times, grid interconnection queues, water for cooling, and critical mineral availability (dysprosium, hafnium and others up more than 125% since February) could cap AI buildout regardless of capital availability. If that happens, the AI capex bust resolves through a supply ceiling rather than a demand collapse — a materially more benign path for credit that my capex-decline criterion would still register as a bust, and that my equity nodes would misprice.

Interconnection between private credit, banks and insurers is a genuine unknown-unknown. The FSB's May 2026 report explicitly names data gaps as one of four vulnerability clusters. Nobody — including regulators — knows the true gross exposure of the banking system to private credit funds, or of life insurers to the credit those funds originated. Losses could be an order of magnitude larger or smaller than the visible default rate implies, and there is no dataset that would resolve this before an event forces disclosure.

The correlation structure between my nodes is more important than any individual probability and I have low confidence in it. Oil, inflation, policy rates, equity drawdown, private credit stress and EM default are being modelled as distinct risks but in a real crisis they are one risk with several names. If the simulation samples them near-independently it will systematically understate joint tail outcomes; if it correlates them fully it will overstate them. The honest answer is that the correlation is state-dependent — near zero in calm regimes and near one in stress — and that regime-switching structure is where most of the real uncertainty lives.

research.state_of_play:
As of late July 2026, the AI sector is in a state of maximum tension between accelerating technical capability and visibly deteriorating financial sentiment.

CAPABILITY (verified). The release cadence compressed further in H1 2026: Claude Opus 4.7 (Apr 16, SWE-bench Verified 87.6%), GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Sonnet 5 (Jun 30), Claude Fable 5 (Jun 9), OpenAI's GPT-5.6 family in three tiers — Luna/Terra/Sol (Jul 9) — and Claude Opus 5 (Jul 24), which took the top of Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index at 61. Benchmarks are saturating unevenly: MMLU/MMLU-Pro are functionally dead above ~88-90%; ARC-AGI-2 is now led at ~85% (above the ~66% average individual human), while the newly released ARC-AGI-3 holds frontier models under 1%; Humanity's Last Exam tops out at ~53% (Claude Fable 5). METR's time-horizon curve remains the most load-bearing metric; reported 50%-reliability horizons for frontier agents range from ~2h17m (GPT-5, May 2026) to claims of ~14.5h, with doubling times variously cited at 4 and 7 months — I could NOT reconcile these sources and treat the level as uncertain even though the trend is robust. Agentic deployment is the defining theme: every major 2026 release is marketed as a worker, not a chatbot.

MONEY (verified, with caveats). Nvidia's Q1 FY2027 (reported May 20, 2026) hit $81.6B revenue, $75.2B data center (+92% YoY), guiding ~$91B for Q2. Big-4 hyperscaler 2026 capex guidance now sits around $600-725B (Amazon ~$200B, Google $175-185B, Meta $125-145B, Microsoft $110-120B), roughly double 2025, with Moody's flagging ~$662B of signed-but-not-commenced lease commitments off balance sheet. Revenue is real but far smaller: OpenAI ~$25B ARR mid-2026 against ~$14B projected 2026 losses and $80-100B/yr of forward compute commitments; multiple outlets report Anthropic overtook OpenAI in run-rate revenue in April 2026 and reached ~$47B by its May 28 Series H — I flag the $30B vs $47B discrepancy as unresolved. Sentiment broke in H1: a June semiconductor selloff erased >$1.3T, and the Nasdaq 100 crossed into correction (>10% drawdown) on July 28.

GEOPOLITICS (verified). The most consequential H1 event may be July 27-28 reporting that a Chinese state-owned entity (Shanghai Aishengna, absorbing SMEE and SiCarrier-affiliated Yuliangsheng teams) began mass production of domestic immersion DUV lithography — five units in 2026, ~20 in 2027, deliveries to SMIC, Hua Hong, CXMT. Domestic EUV remains prototype-stage. Meanwhile the US loosened chip controls (H200 approved for China with a 25% surcharge) but Beijing has largely refused to buy. Chinese open-weight models (DeepSeek-V4, Qwen3.6, Kimi K2.6, GLM, Doubao) reached ~61% of OpenRouter tokens by May 2026 and sit within single digits of Western frontier on engineering benchmarks.

GOVERNANCE (verified). On June 12, 2026, BIS ordered Anthropic to cut off Fable 5 and Mythos 5 to all foreign nationals — the first export-control action against a deployed frontier model; Anthropic took both offline globally; controls lifted June 30. EU AI Act GPAI enforcement powers and fines (up to €15M/3%) switch on August 2, 2026, while the Digital Omnibus (provisional deal May 7, 2026) pushed Annex III high-risk obligations to Dec 2, 2027. In the US, EO 14365 created an AI Litigation Task Force and the March 20 National Policy Framework urged preemption, but Congress has not acted; Colorado's AI Act took effect June 30 and California's TFAIA on Jan 1. The India AI Impact Summit (Feb 16-21) produced a 91-signatory declaration but no binding instrument.

PHYSICAL CONSTRAINTS (verified). TSMC CoWoS is sold out through 2026, scaling from ~35k to 120-140k wafers/month; the supply-demand gap is narrowing 20%→10%. Power is the harder wall: PJM capacity cleared at the $329.17/MW-day cap (vs $28.92 in 2024-25), at least six states have introduced datacenter moratorium bills and seven are restricting tax incentives. Labor evidence remains ambiguous: Census BTOS shows only 17-20% firm-level AI use (32% employment-weighted), and Dallas Fed / Bloomberg-covered research finds no aggregate unemployment effect, though 22-25-year-old software developer employment is down ~20% from 2024.
